Late autumn and early winter benches

Through November and December, our outdoor benches feature cold-hardy stock ready to establish before hard winter frosts arrive. Prominent now are our Winter heather bowls in twenty-five centimetre planters for $22, displaying resilient pink and white tones that persist through winter gloom. Beside them sit dormant Lavender 'Hidcote' pots for $12 and hardy deciduous shrubs resting quietly, their root systems settling steadily into cooling autumn soil.

Midwinter structure and indoor displays

In January and February, focus turns toward protective glasshouse bays and structural evergreens. Hardy fern trios in one-litre pots at $24 provide rich architectural greenery for shaded nooks, while ten-litre Olive trees at $89 lend silver-green structure to sheltered patios. For indoor rooms, our Peace lilies at $28 provide lush foliage under bright indirect light, accompanied by Kitchen herb trios at $14 thriving on warm south-facing kitchen window sills.

Why do we acclimatise our plants outdoors?

Rather than pushing nursery stock into artificial early bloom using supplemental heating, head grower Tomás Reyes and Priya Nair keep our benches open to ambient temperatures. This seasonal exposure hardens cell tissue, strengthens root balls, and prevents the shock that greenhouse-forced plants experience when exposed to domestic gardens. Every pot leaving our benches is conditioned for ordinary outdoor temperature changes and the natural turn of the seasons.

Four categories on our working benches

Our forty-two benches are organized into four primary growing categories: In season, Shrubs and trees, Perennials, and Herbs and indoor. Every bench ticket displays clear specifications including container volume from nine-centimetre pots to ten-litre tubs, light preferences, and mature dimensions. We grow and harden our stock on site so that each plant adapts readily to domestic gardens and indoor rooms without suffering sudden shock.

Stock selections and bench standards

Current selections include our Kitchen herb trio in nine-centimetre pots for $14, Lavender 'Hidcote' in two-litre pots for $12, Panicle hydrangea 'Limelight' in five-litre containers for $38, and Hardy fern trios for $24. For larger spaces, we supply ten-litre Olive trees standing 1.2 metres for $89. Indoor benches feature Peace lilies in seventeen-centimetre pots for $28, alongside Winter heather bowls for $22 and our comprehensive repotting kit for $32.

How do delivery and collection work?

We offer local van delivery across a 15 km radius for a flat fee of $12, with delivery provided free of charge on all orders over $120. Alternatively, you can choose click and collect at checkout and pick up your items directly from our Alder Lane counter during normal hours. All orders are hand-picked from the benches on the morning of dispatch to ensure freshness.

pages.title: Choosing a plant
pages.content:
Selecting a plant should always begin with an honest assessment of your living space rather than decorative impulse. We look at light, space, watering routine, and household companions to find plants a normal home can keep.

LightSpaceTimeCompany

Where will it stand?

Natural light dictates plant survival. A south-facing sill receives intense full sun suited to our Kitchen herb trio or potted Olive trees. An east or west window provides bright indirect daylight where Peace lilies settle comfortably. Shaded courtyards, north-facing balconies, or damp bathroom shelves suit our Hardy fern trio, which prefers to stay away from harsh direct rays. Always observe how natural sunlight moves across your space before making a choice.

Full sun

6+ hoursHerbs, olive, lavender

Bright, indirect

East or west windowPeace lily

Shade

Under 3 hoursHardy ferns

How wide can it grow?

Check both the initial container size and the mature spread of each specimen. A twenty-five centimetre Winter heather bowl remains neat and compact on a doorstep or small terrace table. In contrast, Panicle hydrangea 'Limelight' grows to 1.5 metres high and wide, requiring open ground or a substantial container. Every bench label on Alder Lane states mature dimensions clearly so your plants never outgrow their designated space.

How often will you water?

Watering routines must match your actual schedule. If you tend to water once a week, perennials like Lavender 'Hidcote' and shrubs like Hydrangea flourish under that cadence. If you travel frequently, our ten-litre Olive trees only require watering every ten days once established. If you enjoy daily attentiveness, ferns require compost kept consistently moist, making them rewarding companions for gardeners who check soil moisture regularly.

Who else lives there?

Always consider children and pets before selecting house plants. While ferns, culinary herbs, and lavender are entirely non-toxic, our Peace lily is not pet-safe and must be kept away from chewing animals. If you have questions about specific toxicity or light levels, bring a photo of your room or garden to our plant clinic on Saturdays between 10:00 and 13:00 to discuss options with our nursery team.

pages.title: Aftercare
pages.content:
Caring for a plant continues long after you carry it home from our benches. We provide clear seasonal guidance and a direct follow-up so you know how the plant is settling in its new place.

30-day callSaturday clinic

Spring↘

Feed lightly, repot anything that has filled its pot, move indoor plants back from cold glass.

March – MayFeed lightlyRepot

Summer↘

Water early, check pots weekly, shade tender foliage at midday.

June – AugustWater earlyShade at midday

Autumn↘

Plant shrubs and perennials while the soil is still warm; cut back and mulch.

September – NovemberPlant shrubsMulch

Winter↘

Water less, keep leaves dust-free, move frost-tender pots to shelter.

December – FebruaryWater lessShelter pots

Seasonal care across spring and summer

In spring, inspect garden borders, remove old winter mulch, and cut back shrubs like Panicle hydrangea 'Limelight' to clean lower buds before new growth appears. As summer heat arrives, water plants thoroughly in early morning directly at soil level to prevent fungal issues on leaves. Potted lavender and patio shrubs require weekly soaking, while indoor ferns appreciate daily misting or placement on pebble trays filled with water to maintain ambient humidity.

Autumn care and winter protection

Autumn is the ideal season to plant hardy perennials, ferns, and winter heather while garden soil remains warm from summer sun. Reduce indoor watering as daylight hours contract and central heating is turned on. Before severe winter frosts set in, move outdoor terracotta pots against sheltered walls or lift them onto pot feet so drainage holes do not freeze solid, preventing waterlogged roots during persistent wet spells.

How does the thirty-day follow-up call work?

Following every garden planting visit by Lukas Brandt and our crew, we record your planting scheme in our nursery records. Exactly thirty days later, we contact you by phone or email to check on each specimen's progress. We inquire about watering routines, leaf colour, and new shoot development, offering immediate practical advice if any plant shows signs of transplant stress or slow settling.

What should I do if a plant fails to settle?

Plants are living organisms subject to weather and garden conditions, so we do not promise a set result. If a specimen shows distress during its first thirty days, take a clear photo or bring a foliage cutting to our free Saturday plant clinic between 10:00 and 13:00. Amara Okoye will assess the problem and suggest corrective care. Unused non-plant goods can be returned within 14 days with original receipt.

Questions after the weekend?

Visit the Saturday clinic →

pages.title: About the nursery
pages.content:
Founded in 1998 on Alder Lane in Fernhill by Elena Marsh, Ueki Gardens has spent twenty-eight years growing plants a household can keep. Our six glasshouse bays and forty-two benches focus on dependable, hardy specimens.

Since 199842 benches

Our history on Alder Lane

Elena Marsh founded the nursery in 1998, converting an old market garden into six working glasshouse bays and forty-two plant benches. The name reflects the Japanese word ueki, meaning a plant grown to be kept in a garden or container. Elena liked the term for its quiet focus on cultivated domestic plants, though nothing else across our nursery is Japanese. We remain an independent local nursery growing dependable plants for Fernhill households.

The seven people who look after the nursery

Our team brings dedicated care to every bay. Elena Marsh manages glasshouse propagation and general nursery operations. Tomás Reyes serves as head grower, overseeing our shrubs and trees. Priya Nair manages perennial borders and culinary herbs, while Jonah Feld cares for indoor house plants. Amara Okoye runs aftercare diagnostics and the Saturday plant clinic. Lukas Brandt heads delivery and planting visits, and Mei Lin Ho leads our practical Saturday workshops.

Our philosophy on domestic growing

We choose plants that survive everyday household life rather than fragile exotic showpieces that quickly collapse under central heating or seasonal drafts. Every specimen on our benches spends months hardening off under local outdoor weather conditions in Fernhill. We test plants against realistic watering schedules and room temperatures, so that what you take home has already spent time on our benches under ordinary conditions.

Come and meet us.

Opening hours and holiday closures

We are open daily to the public throughout the year. Our hours are Monday to Saturday from 8:30 to 18:00, and Sunday from 10:00 to 17:00. The nursery is closed on 25 and 26 December for Christmas and on 1 January for New Year's Day. Our click and collect counter operates throughout regular opening hours, allowing you to collect ordered plants, terracotta pots, and compost bags smoothly.

Finding us, parking, and transit

The nursery is situated at 14 Alder Lane, Fernhill. We offer forty free vehicle parking spaces on site, with flat loading trolleys located by the entrance gate to help carry heavy shrubs or compost sacks to your car. If travelling by public transit, take Bus Route 7 and disembark at the Alder Lane stop, positioned fifty paces from our front entrance. Bicycle racks are available beside the main gravel path.

What should I know before visiting?

Well-behaved dogs on leads are welcome throughout our outdoor yard and glasshouse aisles. We advise wearing sensible flat footwear, as gravel pathways are regularly hosed down during bench watering. For inquiries, workshop reservations, or large plant orders, telephone +1 555 014 8820 or email hello@uekigardens.example. For plant health advice, visit our Saturday plant clinic between 10:00 and 13:00 to consult directly with Amara Okoye.

pages.title: Journal
pages.content:
Notes from the Benches is our ongoing record of seasonal shifts, potting trials, and cultivation notes from Fernhill. Here we share practical experiences from our forty-two benches and the gardens that keep our plants.

Dispatches from our forty-two benches

Our four featured journal stories document honest plant experiences from our nursery and local households: A north balcony that keeps ferns now, Herbs on a kitchen sill three winters on, One hydrangea for a shaded front yard, and Monday at the nursery what the weekend leaves. Rather than staged garden portraits, these articles explore real potting mixes, light variations, watering frequencies, and long-term plant health across changing seasons.

Cultivation notes and practical records

Since Elena Marsh opened Ueki Gardens in 1998, we have maintained detailed journals on plant resilience across our six glasshouse bays. Head grower Tomás Reyes logs cold tolerance and root establishment data, while Priya Nair and Jonah Feld record feeding and humidity requirements for domestic spaces. We publish these practical findings so gardeners in Fernhill can make informed, realistic choices for their own courtyards, patios, and window sills.

How can readers submit plant questions?

If you have questions about struggling container specimens or want recommendations for difficult shady borders, send your observations and photographs to hello@uekigardens.example. Amara Okoye reviews customer inquiries weekly and discusses notable cases during our free Saturday morning plant clinic from 10:00 to 13:00 at 14 Alder Lane. Selected seasonal answers are also compiled into future journal entries to help other local gardeners.

posts.title: Monday at the Nursery: What the Weekend Leaves
posts.excerpt: Every Monday morning on Alder Lane reveals exactly how our plants fared over the weekend and what care they need before the benches fill again.
posts.content:
Monday morning at Ueki Gardens begins in quiet contrast to the bustling Saturday crowds. By seven o'clock, the heavy gravel yard at 14 Alder Lane is silent except for the steady drip of condensation falling from the glasshouse eaves. The weekend always leaves its mark across our forty-two benches: wide gaps where potted shrubs once stood, empty timber crates stacked beside the counter, and a light scatter of compost along the main glasshouse aisle. It is the time of the week when our growing team can walk the rows undisturbed, inspecting the specimens that remain and assessing what needs restocking, pruning, or watering.

Elena Marsh founded this nursery in 1998 with a simple principle: we only sell plants that a normal household can keep alive. On Monday mornings, that ethos is visible in every corner of our six glasshouse bays. While retail garden centres rush to conceal empty spaces with flashy, forced blooms shipped from afar, head grower Tomás Reyes takes a measured approach. He wheels a flat timber trolley loaded with potted shrubs down the central aisle, checking root balls and foliage with experienced hands. If a batch of Panicle hydrangea 'Limelight' or potted lavender needs another week of hardening off in the outdoor bays, it stays put until it is truly ready for local gardens.

Nearby, Priya Nair works along the perennial and herb benches, reorganising the Kitchen herb trios and trimming fragrant sprigs of rosemary, thyme, and parsley. When customers buy herbs on a Saturday, they often ask why our nine-centimetre pots look sturdier than supermarket bunches. The answer lies in the unheated bays where they spend their early weeks. Exposure to cool night air and natural daylight produces thicker cell walls and compact root systems that survive on a kitchen sill through three winters or more. Across the aisle, Jonah Feld inspects the indoor benches, wiping the broad leaves of Peace lilies and checking soil moisture with a practiced thumb before deciding whether to water.

Monday is also when our aftercare routine begins in earnest. Lukas Brandt, who runs our local delivery and planting crew, sits down with Amara Okoye to review the installation logbook from the past month. Exactly thirty days after completing a garden planting visit within our 15 km delivery radius, we call or email the homeowner. We ask specific, practical questions about how the planting has settled. Has the soil settled properly around the root ball? Are the lower leaves retaining their colour? How frequently has the household watered during dry spells?

This methodical follow-up is why our customers return year after year. Plants are living organisms that respond directly to soil chemistry, seasonal sunlight, and human habits. When a customer mentions that a newly planted shrub appears sluggish, Amara invites them to bring a cutting or photograph to our free Saturday clinic between 10:00 and 13:00. By midday on Monday, restocked benches gleam in the soft daylight, crates of fresh compost and terracotta pots sit ready by the counter, and Alder Lane settles back into its steady growing rhythm.

posts.title: A north balcony that keeps ferns now
posts.excerpt: A north-facing balcony gets no direct sun, which is exactly what ferns want.
posts.content:
A north-facing balcony gets no direct sun, which is exactly what ferns want. We planted one at the nursery last year to see how it held up.

The ferns sat in grey pots against the wall and were watered twice a week. By the first frost they were fuller than when they arrived.

posts.title: Herbs on a kitchen sill, three winters on
posts.excerpt: A basil, thyme and parsley trio that has outlasted three winters.
posts.content:
Thyme and parsley carry on through winter on a bright sill. Basil does not, and we say so at the counter.

Keep the pots out of draughts, water in the morning, and pinch the tips often.

posts.title: One hydrangea for a shaded front yard
posts.excerpt: A single panicle hydrangea can carry a shaded front yard.
posts.content:
Panicle hydrangeas flower on new wood, so a hard prune in late winter is forgiven. They suit part shade and ordinary soil.

Plant it while the ground is still warm and mulch the first winter.

products.description:
Categorised under Shrubs and trees, Panicle hydrangea 'Limelight' is supplied in a generous five-litre pot for $38. It performs best in positions ranging from full sun to partial shade, reaching a mature height and spread of 1.5 metres. The shrub is fully hardy through cold winters and is non-toxic for domestic gardens. Tomás Reyes monitors these outdoor benches throughout the year to ensure balanced branching and vigorous root development.

Plant your hydrangea into fertile, moisture-retentive soil, incorporating rich garden compost around the root zone. Water weekly during the spring and summer growing season, soaking the ground thoroughly around the base. In late winter or early spring, cut back the previous year's stems to a pair of healthy lower buds. This annual pruning stimulates vigorous new wood that carries dense, conical flower heads emerging lime-green before softening to pale cream.

Local delivery within 15 km is $12, or free on orders exceeding $120, and click and collect from 14 Alder Lane is free.
